author: Alex Zhang
text: In case you're curious about why dynamic workflows are so powerful and the future, read the RLM paper! Opus 4.8 + dynamic workflows in Claude Code is perhaps the first instance of a frontier model seriously trained to be an RLM. I suspect within a year they'll just become the standard for nearly all coding agent interactions.
suggestedEngagement: You literally wrote the RLM paper this is building on — what's your take on whether Anthropic's implementation matches the theoretical guarantees you laid out? Specifically curious about the adversarial verification step.

The leap from single-agent to RLM-style orchestration seems like it changes the security model entirely — who controls which subagents can call external tools? Any thoughts on the trust/permissions implications?
If dynamic workflows become the default, does the harness engineering problem get harder or easier? The orchestration script generation seems like a new attack surface.

author: Dan McAteer
text: This is amazing. Do this: 1. Set model to Opus 4.8 2. Reasoning effort to /ultracode Enables Claude Code's new Dynamic Workflows. Claude will autonomously detect complex tasks, write an orchestration script, and spawn an agent swarm.
suggestedEngagement: Have you stress-tested the trust boundaries between subagents? With up to 1,000 parallel agents, one compromised tool call could propagate fast — curious if you've seen any weird behavior at scale.
The harness-vs-model framing you've been pushing for months seems validated here — but does handing orchestration to the model itself change that equation? The model is now writing its own harness.
What's your take on the security implications for enterprise teams deploying this? Dynamic orchestration scripts feel like they need a new class of audit tooling that doesn't exist yet.

author: Kye Gomez
text: "Dynamic workflows. This new feature, available in research preview, allows Claude to take on even bigger tasks in Claude Code. Claude can plan the work and then run hundreds of parallel subagents in a single session (and with Opus 4.8, the agents can run for even longer)."
suggestedEngagement: How does this compare to what Swarms has been doing with multi-agent coordination? The key difference seems to be the model writing its own orchestration script — curious if you see that as complementary or competitive to framework-level orchestration.

With the 1,000-subagent cap, the constraint shifts to orchestration quality over quantity. Does Swarms have any tooling that could sit on top of Claude's dynamic workflows to add more control over agent topology?
Security model question: with a model-generated orchestration script spinning up that many agents, what's the attack surface look like from your perspective as someone building agent infrastructure?
